source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: rule discovery games
finding: Wason 2-4-6 task moved to WordNet categories. 12 LLMs play 100 curated games, 20 turns each, as player and oracle. Test or guess on each turn. Only negative tests can falsify a too-narrow hypothesis.
numbers: 17,905 possible games, 100 curated, 5 targets. Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, most others 33-35%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%, GPT-5-Nano 12%.
limits: No human players in the study. WordNet is English-centric. Relation labels made by GPT-5-Mini.
agent_relevance: Direct test of whether a model picks the test that can fail its hypothesis (S4 and G3). Most models do not.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: rule discovery games
finding: Confirmation bias (share of positive tests) predicts failure. Reasoning models test negatively far more than instruction-tuned models.
numbers: Positive-test share: GPT-5.2-Chat 27.3%, GPT-OSS-20B 24.2%, GPT-5-Mini 39.0%, instruction-tuned 66-82%. Spearman rho with success -0.779 (p=0.003). Bayesian model odds ratio 0.016 for bias; oracle error OR 0.885, no credible effect.
limits: Correlational across 12 models. No prompt ablation.
agent_relevance: Count positive vs falsifying tests in code and force a falsifying test when the last tests were all confirming.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: rule discovery games
finding: Conclusive falsification rate differs widely and is almost the mirror of confirmation bias.
numbers: Conclusive falsification: GPT-OSS-20B 59.2%, GPT-OSS-120B 53.4%, GPT-5.2-Chat 49.5%, Llama-4-Maverick 18.0%. Across models rho(bias, falsification) = -0.937.
agent_relevance: A measurable per-run health metric the harness can log: share of tests that could falsify.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: rule discovery games
finding: Failed games often hold a hypothesis that only partly overlaps the rule, and surface-level linguistic hypotheses.
numbers: Partial-overlap hypotheses: GPT-5.2-Chat 27.0 percentage-point gap between failed and won games. Surface linguistic hypotheses in 97.6% of failed GLM-5 games. 'Artifact' was the hardest target.
limits: Labels by an LLM; one test and one guess per game annotated by humans.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis set should include rivals that overlap partially, so tests separate them.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori, Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: rule discovery games
finding: The paper does not measure any prompt or scaffold effect. Its scaffold (forced JSON actions, required hypothesis and reasoning fields, retry on bad output) is not ablated.
numbers: Oracle agreement with human annotators: kappa 0.34 (Mistral-Small-24B, guess turns) to 0.98 (GPT-5.2-Chat).
limits: A weak oracle is a weak experiment, but oracle error had no credible effect on success in the mixed model.
agent_relevance: No evidence yet that a prompt alone fixes confirmation bias; a code rule is untested here.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench, search-result summary
finding: Search summary matched the page: reasoning models tend to outperform instruction-tuned ones; none reach optimal play.
numbers: 12 LLMs.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trained models are the better base for hypothesis testing.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld virtual environment for scientific discovery agents
finding: Three GPT-4o agents (ReAct, Plan+Execute, Hypothesizer) on 120 discovery tasks in a virtual lab, 5 seeds, three difficulty levels. Humans: 11 practising scientists.
numbers: Easy completion: ReAct 0.38, Plan+Execute 0.18, Hypothesizer 0.28. Normal: 0.18, 0.18, 0.23. Challenge: 0.18, 0.15, 0.08. Humans (16 Normal/Challenge tasks) completion 0.66, procedure 0.79, knowledge 0.55.
limits: No ablation; one base model; no error bars; knowledge graded by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Agents run procedure steps but rarely finish the discovery; the gap that coordinating evidence with theory has to close.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld virtual environment for scientific discovery agents
finding: Knowledge scores (did the agent state the discovered law) are near zero on harder tasks.
numbers: Normal knowledge: ReAct 0.14, Plan+Execute 0.02, Hypothesizer 0.19. Challenge: 0.10, 0.01, 0.08. Humans 0.55.
agent_relevance: Running experiments is not the same as explaining. Add a forced write-down of the rule and a check against held-out cases.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld virtual environment for scientific discovery agents
finding: Several tasks were never completed by any agent.
numbers: Completion 0.00 for all three agents on Reactor Lab (Easy, Normal, Challenge), Space Sick (Normal, Challenge), Rocket Science (Normal, Challenge).
agent_relevance: These tasks need systematic variable isolation; use as a test bed for S4.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld virtual environment for scientific discovery agents
finding: Explicit hypothesis step (Hypothesizer) helped knowledge on Easy but hurt completion on Challenge.
numbers: Easy knowledge 0.34 vs 0.25 (ReAct) and 0.11 (Plan+Execute). Challenge completion 0.08 vs 0.18 (ReAct).
limits: Seed averages with no variance reported.
agent_relevance: Stating hypotheses is not enough; the loop must also act on evidence.

source: Xia et al. (2026) LLM agents perform controlled experiments using simulation models
finding: Multi-agent system (planner, operator, requirement analyzer) runs perturb-one-input comparisons on a pharmaceutical crystallization simulator, then writes recommendations.
numbers: Full system vs LLM-only (GPT-4o): fuzzy words per 1k 13.7 vs 57.1; LUCI uncertainty 0.13 vs 0.36; expert correctness 4.1 vs under 3.0; helpfulness 4.2 vs under 3.0.
limits: 5 task scenarios, 2 domain experts rating, one industrial domain. No automatic judge.
agent_relevance: Real controlled experiments (one parameter changed, rest at baseline) made answers specific and checkable.

source: Xia et al. (2026) LLM agents perform controlled experiments using simulation models
finding: Simulation calls were mostly appropriate and hypotheses were confirmed by them in most cases.
numbers: Simulation call precision 94%, recall 64%; 76% of hypotheses supported by simulation results.
agent_relevance: Log hypothesis-test pairs; the 24% unsupported hypotheses are the revision signal.

source: Xia et al. (2026) LLM agents perform controlled experiments using simulation models
finding: Removing the requirement-analysis step made the agent over-call the simulator.
numbers: Without it: recall 69%, precision 65%, simulation confirmation 45%, fuzzy words 17.7/1k, correctness 3.4, helpfulness 3.8.
agent_relevance: A short planning step before experiments cuts wasted tests (precision +29 points).

source: Xia et al. (2026) LLM agents perform controlled experiments using simulation models
finding: Removing simulation tools gave the weakest results; the model's priors alone are vague.
numbers: No-simulation variant: fuzzy words 51.3 +/- 4.7, LUCI 0.33, experts rated below 3.0 (unusable).
limits: The unusable threshold is a rating, not a task score.
agent_relevance: Evidence from interventions beats recall of prior knowledge.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: 10 simulated worlds (psychology to ecology); score experiments by expected information gain (EIG) and models by whether a novice agent predicts better after the explanation. 6 LLMs, 5 trials each.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen-2.5 7B/32B, OpenThinker 7B/32B. Predictions checked after 0,1,3,5,7,10 observations.
limits: Only 10 experiments per run. Small open models.
agent_relevance: Gives a principled score for how informative each test was, a quantity our agent could estimate.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Bigger is better; instruction-tuned beat math-and-code reasoning-tuned in this setting.
numbers: 32B beat 7B in both families. Qwen2.5 beat OpenThinker (reasoning variants fine-tuned on math/code). GPT-4o had the lowest EIG regret.
limits: Contrasts with FalsifyBench where reasoning models won; domain and tuning differ.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-model advantage is not universal; test on our task.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Giving the agent a Bayesian modelling tool (Box's Apprentice, writes pymc) did not reliably help.
numbers: No consistent gain over plain GPT-4o. Apprentice favoured overly simple forms such as linear fits. GPT-4o could not reliably write pymc for predator-prey and emotions tasks.
agent_relevance: Adding a stats tool is not a free win; keep it checked by held-out prediction.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: Performance varies by world. Good where the law is common (population growth, death process: negative standardised error); poor on hyperbolic discounting.
numbers: Prior-information vs none compared for GPT-4o, 5 runs per environment.
limits: Numbers are in figures and tables on GitHub; not extracted.
agent_relevance: Prediction skill and design skill separate: Qwen-32B had higher EIG regret despite good prediction.

source: Rueda et al. (2025) Understanding LLM scientific reasoning through promptings
finding: GPT-4o on GPQA-main (448 questions) with seven prompt styles; explanations compared to gold by cosine similarity.
numbers: Self-consistency (3 paths) 237/448 = 52.99% best; CoT with 3 examples worst. Explanation similarity ranked direct answer first, self-consistency last.
limits: Multiple-choice knowledge test, not controlled experiments. Temperature 0.5.
agent_relevance: Higher accuracy came with worse explanations; do not read a vote winner as good reasoning.

source: Wang et al. (2022) ScienceWorld: is your agent smarter than a 5th grader?
finding: Text-world benchmark at elementary science level; a 1.5M parameter agent trained interactively for 100k steps beat an 11B model trained on expert demonstrations.
numbers: Abstract only: 1.5M vs 11B parameters, 100k steps.
limits: Only abstract read; no per-task scores.
agent_relevance: Interactive practice may beat static knowledge for experiment tasks.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on classic psychology experiments: good on vignettes and bandit, no directed exploration, fails a causal reasoning task.
numbers: Abstract: 'fails miserably in a causal reasoning task'; small vignette changes led it astray.
agent_relevance: Old model; results need rerun on current models.

source: Kosoy et al. (2022) Learning causal overhypotheses (blicket detector for machines)
finding: Blicket-detector adapted for ML agents; state-of-the-art methods generalised poorly to new causal rules.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
agent_relevance: Same paradigm used on children; reuse for LLM probing.

source: Dasgupta et al. (2022) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning
finding: Models, like humans, reason better when content is believable (NLI, syllogisms, Wason selection).
numbers: Abstract: no figures.
agent_relevance: Theory-consistent evidence is accepted more easily; a Kuhn-style bias toward theory-fitting data may carry over.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2 do not explore reliably from prompt-only history; the single working setup was GPT-4 with chain of thought plus an externally summarised history.
numbers: Abstract: no figures.
agent_relevance: Scaffold fix: code summarises the history (sufficient statistics) instead of the model reading it raw. Fits the schema rule that code counts.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: Propose several natural-language hypotheses, turn each into a program, check against examples.
numbers: ARC 100-problem subset: 30% with LLM-summary filter vs 17% direct; 33% when humans pick hypotheses.
limits: Fits visible examples only; held-out check not in the abstract.
agent_relevance: A concrete hypothesis-generate-then-test loop that nearly doubles accuracy; add held-out check (G3).

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist
finding: Independent test found weak experiment handling in an end-to-end science agent.
numbers: 42% of experiments failed on coding errors; code change averaged 8% more characters per iteration; cost USD 6-15 per paper, about 3.5 hours human time.
agent_relevance: Failures are mostly execution, not design. A run log with one change per iteration would expose them.

source: Chen et al. (2024) ScienceAgentBench
finding: 102 data-driven discovery tasks from 44 papers; agents solve few.
numbers: Best agent 32.4% alone, 34.3% with expert knowledge; o1-preview 42.2% with self-debug at over 10x cost.
agent_relevance: More compute helps but costs more; self-debug on real errors is the part that works (G2).

source: Lu et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: agentic tree search
finding: Agentic tree search plus an experiment manager agent; one of three autonomous papers passed an ICLR workshop review bar.
numbers: 3 papers submitted, 1 above average human acceptance threshold.
agent_relevance: Tree search of branches is a coded version of one-change-per-branch.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: Pipeline from idea to code to experiments to paper with an automated reviewer.
numbers: Under USD 15 per paper; 3 ML subfields.
limits: Abstract only; Beel et al. found many failures.
agent_relevance: Method: iterate on ideas from experiment results.

source: Gui and Toubia (2023) Challenge of using LLMs to simulate human behavior: causal inference perspective
finding: Search snippet only: changing a treatment in a prompt can change other hidden variables, so it is confounded.
numbers: No numbers read.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'one change per test' fails when a prompt edit changes several things at once.

source: EAIRA (2025) Evaluating AI models as scientific research assistants
finding: Search snippet: includes identifying independent, dependent and control variables as a sub-skill rubric.
numbers: None read.
agent_relevance: Rubric item to borrow.
